source: សៀវភៅស្ដីពីដំណាំដំឡូងមី (Book on Cassava), Part 2, UNDP-supported capacity-building programme for cassava, March 2015, Section 10.4
text:
To export cassava products from Cambodia, exporters apply for a Certificate of Origin (CO) from the Ministry of Commerce; the specific CO form required depends on the destination country and applicable trade agreement. The source lists the CO forms available: Form N; Form A; Form B225; Form D (export to ASEAN countries); Form E (ASEAN-China Free Trade Area); Form AJ (ASEAN-Japan); Form AK (ASEAN-Korea); and Form ANZ (ASEAN-Australia-New Zealand). For cassava exports to China specifically, the source specifies that exporters should use CO Form E (the ASEAN-China Free Trade Area Preferential Tariff Certificate of Origin, a combined declaration and certificate). A specimen of Form E is reproduced in the source, showing the required fields: exporter and consignee details, transport/route details, item description with HS code, origin criteria, gross weight/value (FOB), invoice details, an exporter declaration of origin, and an official certification block completed by the issuing authority.

CO applications can be submitted either in person (paper application) or online via the Ministry of Commerce's online CO portal at www.ico.moc.gov.kh.

Documents typically required to support a CO application include: the CO application form; company registration/patent (business registration) documents; commercial invoice; packing list; airway bill or bill of lading (depending on transport mode); phytosanitary/fumigation inspection results where applicable; a fumigation certificate if the shipment requires fumigation; sales contract; and a producer's declaration of origin (an additional business license may be needed if goods are sourced from a separate supplier rather than the exporter's own production).
caveat: This is new, directly actionable content for the knowledge base covering Cambodia's cassava-export certification pathway to China. The list of supporting-document requirements was compiled from a source passage listing bullet items in a somewhat dense format; treat the list as broadly representative rather than an exhaustive, officially guaranteed checklist, and confirm current requirements with the Ministry of Commerce or GDA before relying on it for an actual export transaction, since procedures can change over time.
